citation.author: Raffaelli, Quentin; Mills, Caitlin; Christoff, Kalina
citation.title: The Knowns and Unknowns of Boredom: A Review of the Literature
citation.note: Received 6 April 2016; accepted 16 February 2017; published online 28 March 2017; print issue year 2018 (as given in the bibliographic header).

discipline: cognitive psychology / cognitive neuroscience (synthesizes behavioral, fMRI, and EEG literatures on boredom)
thesis: Synthesizes correlates of boredom into 'known' (consistently observed: attentional mismatch, task-unrelated thought frequency, overestimated time perception, reduced agency, negative valence, DMN activation) versus 'unknown' (inconsistently observed: arousal direction, hippocampus/insula recruitment, attribution-boredom causal direction) categories, scoped explicitly to state (not trait) boredom. Diagnoses two separable causes of field-wide inconsistency -- non-standardized operationalization of a single construct, and the unresolved, evidence-suggested possibility that boredom is a heterogeneous family of distinct subtypes -- and recommends addressing both, without resolving which explanation is correct.
sections: Introduction: What is boredom? (p.2451) -- motivating open questions; roadmap aim stated

Table 1 + Definitions and functions of boredom (p.2452) -- psychodynamic/existentialist/arousal/cognitivist schools; Mikulas and Vodanovich (1993) and Eastwood et al. (2012) definitions; Bench and Lench (2013) functional account

Boredom as an attentional failure (pp.2452-2454) -- Mismatch hypothesis (arousal/task-difficulty mismatch, flow contrast, Freeman et al. 2004 EEG-engagement vigilance study, educational/ZPD examples); Task-unrelated thoughts; Attributions of attention
Time perception (pp.2454-2455) -- overestimation of elapsed time as a consistent correlate
Agency (p.2455) -- reduced perceived freedom to choose one's activity

Dimensions of affect (pp.2455-2457) -- Valence (consistently negative); Arousal (inconsistent; directional fractionation hypothesis); Different boredom types (Goetz et al. 2014 five-category taxonomy)

Neural correlates (pp.2457-2459) -- Brain regions (Ulrich et al. 2014; Mathiak et al. 2013; Danckert and Merrifield 2016: convergent DMN, divergent hippocampus/insula); Neural oscillations (EEG alpha/beta, engagement indices)
Mood and fatigue (pp.2459-2460) -- flagged as 'probable' correlates only
Conclusion (p.2460) -- recommends standardized operationalization and empirical testing/validation of a boredom-type taxonomy

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: explicit scoping decision -- review 'encompasses the correlates of boredom as a transient state, rather than boredom as a trait'; trait boredom appears only as an occasional secondary covariate (Danckert and Allman 2005; Merrifield and Danckert 2014)

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: narrow treatment as what the Boredom Proneness Scale (Farmer and Sundberg 1986) operationalizes; cited as a trait-level covariate predicting time-overestimation and heart rate, not developed independently

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: dedicated subsection; explicit terminological correction away from 'mind-wandering' toward 'task-unrelated thoughts' (citing Christoff et al. 2016)

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: organizing frame for the paper's middle third ('Boredom as an attentional failure'); Critcher and Gilovich's metacognitive-appraisal argument

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: Bench and Lench's (2013) functional/adaptive-emotion account adopted directly into the review's working definition of boredom

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: Csikszentmihalyi's flow as boredom's structural opposite throughout the mismatch-hypothesis discussion; Ulrich et al. (2014) fMRI directly contrasts flow, boredom, and anxiety conditions

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: dedicated subsection; overestimation of elapsed time named among the review's most consistent correlates

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: single glancing citation to Frankl's (1992) existentialist account as one of several competing definitional schools; not adopted or returned to

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.treatment: BPS (Farmer and Sundberg 1986) and Goetz et al. (2014) experience-sampling ratings surveyed from the literature; none administered by this review itself

measures.label: heart rate / HRV
measures.treatment: London et al. (1972) and Merrifield and Danckert (2014) autonomic-arousal findings surveyed; central to the directional fractionation hypothesis

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.treatment: vigilance-task decrement (Freeman et al. 2004), attentional blink, SART, and Stroop-task findings surveyed as attention/mood-linked performance measures

measures.label: EEG alpha/theta power
measures.treatment: Oswald's (1962) alpha hypothesis and the beta/(alpha+theta) engagement-index formula (Pope, Bogart, and Bartolome 1995) surveyed; explicitly flagged as scarce, high-value future-work territory

concepts: mismatch hypothesis (arousal/task-difficulty mismatch as boredom's proximal cause)
Yerkes-Dodson law (optimal arousal for task performance)
directional fractionation hypothesis (Lacey 1959; Lacey and Lacey 1970) -- EDA and heart rate diverge in direction during boredom
Circumplex Model of Affect (Russell 1980; Posner et al. 2005) -- valence x arousal space boredom does not cleanly fit
default mode network (DMN) recruitment during internally-directed attention/boredom
engagement index (beta power / [alpha power + theta power]; Pope, Bogart, and Bartolome 1995)
task-unrelated thought (terminological alternative to 'mind-wandering', per Christoff et al. 2016)
five-type taxonomy of boredom (Goetz et al. 2014): indifferent, calibrating, searching, reactant, apathetic
interlocutors: John Eastwood, Alexandra Frischen, Mark Fenske, Daniel Smilek (2012) -- 'The Unengaged Mind'; supplies the review's adopted working definition of boredom and its attentional-failure framing throughout
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1975, 1990, 1991, 1996, 2000) -- flow theory; the arousal-mismatch contrast pole against which boredom is defined
Shane Bench and Heather Lench (2013) -- 'On the Function of Boredom'; functional/adaptive-emotion account adopted into the working definition
Thomas Goetz et al. (2007, 2013, 2014) -- five-type experience-sampling taxonomy of boredom; central evidence for the heterogeneity hypothesis
James Danckert and Colleen Merrifield (2014, 2016) -- psychophysiological signature of boredom; four-condition fMRI study (DMN/insula dissociation)
Reinhard Pekrun and colleagues (2002, 2010, 2014) -- control-value theory of academic emotions; academic-boredom achievement outcomes
Wijnand van Tilburg and Eric Igou (2012, 2016) -- meaning/challenge-based differentiation of boredom from other negative emotions
Viktor Frankl (1992) -- existentialist meaninglessness account of boredom, cited once and not adopted
Kalina Christoff, Zachary Irving, Kieran Fox, R. Nathan Spreng, Jessica Andrews-Hanna (2016) -- spontaneous-thought framework motivating the 'task-unrelated thought' terminological choice
Richard Farmer and Norman Sundberg (1986) -- Boredom Proneness Scale
Manuela Ulrich, Jochen Keller, Klaus Hoenig, Christiane Waller, Georg Gron (2014) -- fMRI study contrasting flow, boredom, and anxiety
Klaus Mathiak, Martin Klasen, Mikhail Zvyagintsev, Rene Weber, Klaus Mathiak (2013) -- fMRI study of boredom during first-person-shooter video-game play
tensions: PRIMARY DEBATE-AXIS POSITION -- 'boredom as unified construct <-> heterogeneous family (Raffaelli review)' (this cluster's named axis, primarily grounded here): R,M&C do NOT resolve this axis to either pole. They diagnose the field's inconsistencies (chiefly around arousal and recruited brain regions) as compatible with TWO separable explanations -- (a) non-standardized operationalization of a single, unified construct across studies (a measurement-noise account that keeps boredom unified in principle), and (b) genuine construct heterogeneity, i.e. distinct boredom subtypes with different antecedents and signatures (a heterogeneous-family account). They treat (b) as a serious, evidence-backed hypothesis -- citing Goetz et al.'s (2014) five-category experience-sampling taxonomy as preliminary support (pp.2456-2457) -- and their own forward recommendation commits them to testing it: 'arriving at an empirically validated taxonomy of different types of boredom' is named as one of two necessary next steps (p.2451, abstract; p.2460). But they repeatedly hedge this claim ('preliminary evidence suggests...', 'if different types of boredom do indeed exist...', p.2451, p.2460), stopping short of asserting heterogeneity as established. Net position: an explicitly UNRESOLVED, dual-hypothesis diagnosis that treats heterogeneity as the more novel and forward-pointing (though unconfirmed) explanation, rather than a flat defense of construct unity.

Subjective arousal reports (boredom as low-arousal: Geiwitz 1966; Pekrun et al. 2002) vs. autonomic arousal measures (boredom as high-arousal: London et al. 1972; Merrifield and Danckert 2014) -- formalized as the directional fractionation hypothesis (Lacey 1959; Lacey and Lacey 1970); R,M&C treat this as one of the field's two most important open contradictions, feeding directly into the cluster's 'self-report <-> physiological-marker as ground truth' axis (pp.2455-2457).

Explicit methodological bracketing of situational/state boredom against trait boredom: the review commits to state boredom as its sole object of study (p.2452), which sharpens its findings but means none of its 'known/unknown' correlates should be read as claims about trait boredom proneness.

Internal tension in the neural-correlates literature: hippocampus activation (Ulrich et al. 2014) vs. hippocampus deactivation (Mathiak et al. 2013) vs. no reported hippocampal involvement (Danckert and Merrifield 2016) under three different operational definitions of boredom -- offered by R,M&C as direct evidence that operationalization inconsistency, not just noisy measurement, may be driving apparently conflicting neuroimaging results (p.2458).
